summary: This standards-track RFC defines a Port Control Protocol option, THIRD_PARTY_ID, used together with the THIRD_PARTY option from RFC 6887. It identifies a third party when that party's IP address alone is not enough to create the requested mappings in a PCP-controlled device.

eli5.summary: Asking a doorman to open a door for someone else, and giving a name when an address is not enough.

questions: what is the pcp third_party_id option
subtitle: An extra identifier for PCP requests made on behalf of a host that its IP address alone cannot identify.

tldr.problem: A PCP client can name another host with the THIRD_PARTY option, but some carrier-grade NATs reuse private addresses across subscribers, so an IP address alone does not say which host is meant.
tldr.mechanism: The THIRD_PARTY_ID option (option code 13) carries a deployment-specific identifier, such as a tunnel ID, that is used together with the THIRD_PARTY address to find the right NAT mapping.
tldr.outcome: A PCP server can now tell hosts with overlapping addresses apart. The option is only valid with MAP and PEER requests, and it adds three new result codes. The RFC updates RFC 6887.

today: RFC 7843 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2016. It updates RFC 6887 and has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: The Problem with Address-Only Third Parties
sections.content:
The Port Control Protocol (PCP, RFC 6887) controls how packets are translated or forwarded by a PCP-controlled device such as a NAT or a firewall. RFC 6887 already defines a THIRD_PARTY option that carries the IP address of a host on whose behalf the PCP client is making a request.

That is not always enough. Some Carrier-Grade NAT (CGN) deployments do not tell internal hosts apart by IP address alone. When a CGN supports overlapping private or shared address spaces for the hosts of different subscribers, it also uses another identifier, for example the ID of the tunnel between the CGN and the subscriber. In those cases the address in the THIRD_PARTY option cannot demultiplex connections from internal hosts.

The THIRD_PARTY_ID option carries that additional identifier. It is defined for the PCP opcodes MAP and PEER and is used together with the THIRD_PARTY option.
sections.eli5: Two kids on different streets can both live at number 5. Just saying the number is not enough, so you also say the street.

sections.title: The L2-Aware NAT Scenario
sections.content:
Both scenarios in the RFC are refinements of one basic setup. A carrier runs a CGN with a co-located PCP server, plus a PCP Interworking Function (IWF) that contains a PCP client serving many subscribers. The CGN acts as an L2-aware NAT: unlike a standard NAT, its mapping table entries hold a subscriber identifier in addition to the source IP address.

Internal hosts use private addresses, there is no NAT between a host and the CGN, and addresses overlap between subscribers. The subscriber's Customer Premises Equipment (CPE) works as a Layer 2 bridge. A natural extra identifier is the ID of the tunnel connecting the CGN to the subscriber's network. The IWF puts the host's address in a THIRD_PARTY option and the tunnel ID in a THIRD_PARTY_ID option. The CGN needs the same information to translate packet addresses and to forward packets into subscriber-specific tunnels.

How the IWF manages mappings, such as extending their lifetime, is outside the scope of the RFC.
sections.eli5: The phone company's big shared mailroom has to know which building a letter belongs to as well as the apartment number, because many buildings have an apartment 5.

sections.title: Two Example Deployments
sections.content:
The RFC gives two examples and says there may be others. The option is restricted to cases where it is needed to identify an internal host beyond what the THIRD_PARTY option provides.

In the carrier-hosted UPnP IGD-PCP IWF scenario, the subscriber asks for port mappings using UPnP-IGD (RFC 6970). The IWF is offered as a service rather than embedded in the subscriber's router. It either uses the ID of the tunnel the UPnP message arrived in directly as the THIRD_PARTY_ID, or looks that ID up at the Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) server. For the lookup, the Broadband Remote Access Server (BRAS) registers the subscriber's tunnel IDs at the AAA server, and the IWF asks for the ID of the tunnel between the BRAS and the CGN.

In the carrier web portal scenario, the subscriber uses HTTP(S), by hand in a browser or automatically from applications. The portal, a web server combined with a PCP client, queries the AAA server for the BRAS-to-CGN tunnel ID and uses it as the THIRD_PARTY_ID.
sections.eli5: You can ask the doorman through a speaker phone or by filling in a form on a website. Either way, the helper looks up your building's code before telling him.

sections.title: The THIRD_PARTY_ID Option Format
sections.content:
The option uses the standard PCP option layout from RFC 6887: an option code, a reserved field, an option length and then the data. Its option code is 13. It is valid for the MAP and PEER opcodes, may appear in a request, may appear in a response only if it was in the matching request, and may occur at most once. Its length is variable, with a maximum of 1016 octets.

The THIRD_PARTY_ID field holds a deployment-specific identifier of the realm of a NAT map entry. It has no other meaning and is not tied to any particular identifier type. The client and server must agree on what it contains, and the client need not understand how the server uses it. If the ID comes from an existing standard, that standard's encoding rules must be followed. For an L2TPv3 session ID, it is encoded as in the L2TPv3 session header, so the device can compare octet by octet.

PCP option data comes in whole octets. An ID that is not, such as a 20-bit MPLS label, is padded with 0 bits up to the byte boundary, then the padding rules of RFC 6887 apply.

The option code is in the mandatory-to-process range (0-127). A server that supports the option processes the request, so a client should not include it unless a mapping without it is impossible.
sections.eli5: It is a small label stuck on the request. The label can say anything the helper and the doorman agreed on, as long as it is written the way they expect.

sections.title: Client and Server Behavior
sections.content:
A client MAY include THIRD_PARTY_ID in a MAP or PEER request, and it MUST be used together with the THIRD_PARTY option. The padding rules above apply.

On the server, the option is in the mandatory-to-process range, so a server that does not support it MUST return UNSUPP_OPTION. Three new result codes cover the other failures, all described as long lifetime errors:

  • THIRD_PARTY_ID_UNKNOWN (24): the identifier is unknown or unavailable to the server.
  • THIRD_PARTY_MISSING_OPTION (25): one of THIRD_PARTY and THIRD_PARTY_ID is missing when both are expected.
  • UNSUPP_THIRD_PARTY_ID_LENGTH (26): the option length is not supported.

For a valid request, processing follows RFC 6887, except that the mapping table is accessed using the combination of the THIRD_PARTY address and the THIRD_PARTY_ID, which together select the internal address and internal realm of a NAT map entry. If several tunnel technologies are used, their ID spaces may overlap, so precautions are needed; one example is using a separate PCP client and server pair per technology.

When a client gets one of the three new errors back, it SHOULD report an error, with where to report it set by policy.
sections.eli5: If the doorman does not know the street, or the form is missing a part, he says so with a specific code, and the helper tells someone about the problem.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Because the option is used with THIRD_PARTY, the security considerations in Section 18.1.1 of RFC 6887 apply. In particular, the network carrying PCP messages must be sufficiently protected, and PCP authentication (RFC 7652) is RECOMMENDED unless the network already has appropriate authentication.

The identifier's type and length depend on the deployment, and it might carry privacy-sensitive information. Identifiers without such concerns are RECOMMENDED, and means to prevent unauthorized access MUST be in place. In the example scenarios, access to the web portal or the UPnP IGD-PCP IWF MUST be authenticated. The identifier MUST only be accessible by the network operator and handled on operator equipment, so the subscriber triggers the message but an operator-controlled entity fills in the option.
sections.eli5: The street label might reveal where someone lives, so only the phone company's own helpers should ever write it down.

sections.title: IANA Allocations
sections.content: IANA allocated PCP option code 13 (THIRD_PARTY_ID) in the mandatory-to-process range. It also allocated three PCP result codes: 24 (THIRD_PARTY_ID_UNKNOWN), 25 (THIRD_PARTY_MISSING_OPTION) and 26 (UNSUPP_THIRD_PARTY_ID_LENGTH).
sections.eli5: The official list of codes got four new entries, one for the label and three for the things that can go wrong.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set as specified in Section 7.3 of RFC 6887.

fields.name: Option Length
fields.desc: Length of the identifier; variable, maximum 1016 octets.

fields.name: THIRD_PARTY_ID
fields.desc: Variable-length, deployment-specific identifier, padded to a whole number of octets.

items.label: THIRD_PARTY_ID_UNKNOWN
items.desc: The identifier is unknown or unavailable to the PCP server.

items.label: THIRD_PARTY_MISSING_OPTION
items.desc: THIRD_PARTY or THIRD_PARTY_ID is missing when both are expected.

items.label: UNSUPP_THIRD_PARTY_ID_LENGTH
items.desc: The received option length is not supported.
